n: Dated to the eleventh year (about 587–586 BC), around Jerusalem’s fall, this begins three chapters about Tyre, the wealthy Phoenician trading city on the coast of modern Lebanon.

f.g: About 587/586 BC; the month is not given in the Hebrew.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

n: Tyre rejoiced: “Aha! Jerusalem, the gateway of the nations, is broken. Now her trade will come to me.” Tyre saw Judah’s disaster as a business opportunity.

f.g: Tyre, a Phoenician port partly on an island just off the coast; famous for sea trade and purple dye.
Jerusalem controlled inland trade routes.

n: God is against Tyre and will send nation after nation against her like waves crashing on her island.

f.w: as the sea causeth his waves to come up
f.g: A fitting image for an island city—many waves over a long time.

n: Her walls and towers will fall; God will scrape her down to bare rock—a play on Tyre’s name, which means “rock.”

f.g: Tyre (Hebrew Tsor) means “rock.”

n: She will become a place where fishermen spread their nets to dry—a striking image of a once-busy port reduced to nothing.

f.w: a place for the spreading of nets

n: Her “daughters”—towns on the mainland—will be put to the sword.

f.w: her daughters which are in the field
f.g: Tyre’s dependent settlements on the mainland.

n: God names the first wave: Nebuchadnezzar, “king of kings,” coming from the north with a great army.

f.g: A spelling closer to the Babylonian Nabû-kudurri-uṣur.
A title used by Mesopotamian emperors.

n: He will destroy the mainland towns and build siege works against Tyre.
Battering rams will strike her walls, and axes will cut down her towers.

f.g: Battering rams.

n: His horses will raise clouds of dust, and the walls will shake as his chariots thunder through breached gates.

f.g: A gap broken in a city wall.

n: He will trample her streets, kill her people, and topple her mighty pillars.

f.g: Probably her sacred pillars—Tyre’s temples had famous pillars.

n: Note the shift to “they”: enemies will loot Tyre’s wealth and throw her stones, timber, and rubble into the sea. Alexander the Great did exactly this in 332 BC, using the ruins of mainland Tyre to build a causeway to the island.

f.w: they shall lay thy stones and thy timber and thy dust in the midst of the water
f.g: Fulfilled strikingly in Alexander’s siege of 332 BC.

n: Tyre’s songs and harps—the sounds of a prosperous party city—will fall silent.

f.w: the sound of thy harps shall be no more heard

n: She will be bare rock for drying nets and never rebuilt as she was. Old Tyre’s glory never returned, though a later town grew nearby.

f.w: thou shalt be built no more
f.g: The great city-state never regained its former power.

n: Coastal lands will shake at the noise of her fall.

f.g: Coastlands and islands of the Mediterranean that traded with Tyre.

n: The sea-kings will step down from their thrones, remove their royal robes, and sit trembling on the ground in mourning.

f.g: Rulers of other trading cities.

f.w: they shall clothe themselves with trembling

n: They will lament: “How you are destroyed, famous city of sailors, once mighty on the sea and feared by all!”

f.g: A funeral lament formula.

n: The coastlands will tremble at her collapse.

f.g: Your end.

n: God will make Tyre an empty ruin, covered by the ocean depths.

f.w: bring up the deep upon thee
f.g: The primeval deep, a symbol of chaos and death.

n: He will send her down to the pit—the realm of the dead—with ancient peoples, while he gives glory to the land of the living (Israel).

f.g: The grave or underworld (Sheol).

f.w: I shall set glory in the land of the living
f.g: Possibly “you will no longer have a place in the land of the living.”

n: Tyre will come to a terrifying end; people will search for her, but she will never be found again as she was.

f.w: yet shalt thou never be found again
